Yes. 

The manipulation of time in the story is masterfully balanced to serve its emotional arc. The first half uses **compression of time**, summarizing roughly a dozen years—from the characters' sophomore year of college through a decade of post-graduate life—in just a few paragraphs. Through carefully chosen anecdotes and a quick summary of their diverging paths, the narrator efficiently establishes Q's seemingly effortless perfection and his own lingering feelings of inadequacy ("Ten years on, I wrote copy for a dental-supply company. I was, by most measures, fine. I was solid.").

Once the narrator steps into the hotel pool, the pacing shifts dramatically into real-time and **stretching of time**. A conversation that lasts only a couple of minutes takes up the entire second half of the story. At the climax of the conversation—when Dana misunderstands Q and thinks she got the promotion—time stretches even further to capture a fraction of a second in granular detail: *"Here was the second where he could set it right... I watched him decide, and I watched him fail to decide, and I watched the failure become a decision on its own."* 

This contrast is completely appropriate: compressing the first twelve years builds the weight of the narrator's long-held obsession with Q, which makes stretching out the brief, agonizing moment of Q's failure feel earned, suspenseful, and deeply impactful.
